title: Fill the Rectangle
idea: (x + a)(x + b) is the area of a rectangle split into four pieces, so expanding multiplies every term in one bracket by every term in the other, and (x + a)² has two middle strips.
misconceptions: Squares each term: (x + r)² = x² + r²
Gets the sign of a product wrong
Multiplies d by k as well in k(x + r)² + d

estimate.basis: 150 spoken words a minute, plus each pause, 0.8 s for each cue and 2 s for each tap question with its longer feedback line. The two figures are the two recall versions; with no prerequisite explainer there is one recall version, so they are the same. Player turns are player-paced and not counted.

notes: Foundations is prior learning (FAL-953), so this runs 4–6 minutes, not 6–8, and some sections are short.

No prerequisite explainer. The recall section is one tap question on what students bring from earlier school (expanding a single bracket), with no callback line, so it has a single `beats` list instead of `watched` and `not_watched`, and both length figures are the same.

No second-method section: the map lists no methods. The question type's four (distribute, grid, square pattern, number check) are all one idea here: the grid is the picture, distributing is the written form, the square pattern is the recap line, and the number check closes every example.
The rectangle in the big idea is written as a text grid. A drawn one would be better; it needs a figure board item, raised on FAL-953 for phase 2.
The misconception "multiplies the factor in front into only the first bracket term" is met in example 3, where the 2 multiplies all three terms, but it is not given its own wrong answer.
Example 3 is a two-part course-style item (SL2.6, vertex form to expanded form, and the y-intercept), as FAL-953 allows for Foundations.
Live numbers for the turns come from fn-pre-expand (game/engine/situations/expand.gd); the fallbacks are fixed and worked below.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Tess again. Somebody's put a hole through the side of my shed, and I'm patching it with a sheet of tin.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: No idea who. The ute parked next to it has a dent the exact same shape, mind.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: To cut the patch I need its area. And the sides have letters in them.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: First, one you brought with you from school. Tap the answer.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Three x plus twelve. The three multiplies everything in the bracket.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: The three multiplies everything inside the bracket. Three lots of x, and three lots of four. Three x plus twelve.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Here's the sheet. One side is x plus three, the other is x plus two. Area is one side times the other.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Hard to multiply as it stands, so cut it up. Split each side where the plus is, x and three one way and x and two the other, and you've got four pieces.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: The big square, x by x, is x squared. A strip x by two is two x, a strip three by x is three x, and the little corner, three by two, is six.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Add the pieces. When you multiply out brackets like this, you expand them.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Two x and three x are like terms: same letter, same power. So they go together. x squared, plus five x, plus six.

board.write: like terms: the same letter to the same power

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Every term in one bracket, times every term in the other. Bits on the bench, then bolt them together.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Want to know it's right? Try a number. Put x equals one into both, and four times three is twelve, and one plus five plus six is twelve. Same both ways.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: I patched a roof once without measuring. Lovely job. Covered half the roof and most of the neighbour's.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Step one: what we're finding. Expand x plus four, times x plus five.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Step two: the four pieces. x times x, x squared. x times five, five x. Four times x, four x. Four times five, twenty.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: That's it. Two terms times two terms. Four pieces, every time.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Each of the two terms in the first bracket meets each of the two in the second. Two times two, four pieces.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Step three: collect the like terms. Five x and four x make nine x. So it's x squared plus nine x plus twenty.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Step four: check with a number. With x as one, five times six is thirty, and one plus nine plus twenty is thirty.

intro.speaker: tin-can-tess
intro.say: Your go. Four pieces, then collect.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Sweet as. Bits on the bench, and it all went together.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Choice. And you checked it, too.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Count your pieces. Two terms times two terms makes four.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Check it with a number. Put x equals one into both. Do they match?

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Now a square patch. x plus four on both sides, so it's x plus four, all squared. Squared means times itself, so write it as two brackets first.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Eight x. Two strips of four x, one down the side and one along the top.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Picture the square. There's a strip of four x down one side, and another along the top. Two strips, eight x.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: So it's x squared, plus eight x, plus sixteen. Those two middle strips are the bit everyone leaves out.

problem.setup: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2(x − 3)² + 1.

parts.text: Write down the coordinates of the y-intercept of the graph of f.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Last one's set out like the exam papers. Two parts, letters down first.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Here's f. Take x minus three, square it, times by two, then add one.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Part a says show that. They've given you the answer, so your job is to get there from f, one step at a time, and land exactly on their line.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Square the bracket first. x minus three, times x minus three. x squared, minus three x, minus three x, and minus three times minus three.

ask.prompt: Why is the last piece +9, not −9?
choices: Every term in a square is positive
The 2 in front makes it positive

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: The last piece is minus three times minus three. Negative times negative is positive, so it's plus nine.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: That's x squared minus six x plus nine. Now the two in front multiplies all three terms. The plus one goes on after, and the two never touches it.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: That's their line, so we stop.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Part b says write down. The y-intercept is where x is zero, so every x term goes and nineteen is left. Zero, nineteen. And it checks against the start: two lots of nine, plus one.

sections.misconception: Gets the sign of a product wrong

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Somebody taped this to my shed door. Cheeky. One line's a bit off. Find it.

ask.prompt: Tap the line with the slip.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: That's the one. Minus five times two is minus ten, not plus ten.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Check the sign of each piece on the second line. What's minus five times two?

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Try x equals one. The brackets give minus four times three, minus twelve, and their answer gives one minus three plus ten, which is eight. No match.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Line through it, and fix the sign. x squared minus three x minus ten. Now x equals one gives minus twelve both ways.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: I keep every bolt I've stripped in a tin. Half of them are sign slips.

intro.speaker: tin-can-tess
intro.say: Your go, and no help on the first try. Square the bracket first, and the number in front multiplies every term.

fallback.setup: The function f is defined by f(x) = 3(x − 2)² + 5.

parts.text: Write down the coordinates of the y-intercept of the graph of f.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Every term, every sign. That'd hold.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Choice. You landed right on their line.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Check the last piece of your square. What's negative times negative?

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: The number in front multiplies every term in the bracket. Did it reach all three?

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: So. To expand, multiply every term in one bracket by every term in the other, then collect the like terms. A square is two brackets, with two middle strips. Then check with a number.

board.write: (x + a)(x + b): every term × every term

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Next time we run it backwards. You get the area, and you find the sides.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: The shed's patched, by the way. And the ute's owner has offered to pay for the tin. Funny, that.
